BY Pr e s id e n t  Ba r a c k Ob a ma  (2017). Because the recess appointments 
power creates an obvious path for presidents to seek to evade the Senate’s 
role in the confirmation process, it has been a recurrent source of 
interbranch friction. Among the more dramatic flare-ups, in 1903 Theodore 
Roosevelt used a moment’s intersession recess to make 193 executive 
branch appointments, literaUy between two raps of a gavel.
Among recent presidents prior to the Trump Administration, Ba-rack 
Obama was—in terms of numbers—the least active “recess appointer,” 
having made only 32 such designations in eight years. (By way of contrast. 
President Reagan was the most active—having made 160 such intersession 
appointments alone over the course of his two Administrations; George W. 
Bush was the most active intrasession appointer, having made 141 such 
appointments over eight years. Id.) Obama appointments during 2010 and 
2012, however, to the National Labor Relations Board stirred considerable 
controversy that led to the Supreme Court’s first interpretation of the 
recess appointment power’s scope.
In March 2010, Obama appointed labor lawyer Craig Becker to the 
NLRB during a two-week intrasession Senate recess. A Republican 
filibuster had prevented the Senate from taking a floor vote on Mr. Becker, 
whom the president had nominated to the NLRB eight-and-a-half months 
earlier. The president resubmitted the Becker nomination on January 26, 
2011, but the filibuster persisted. Republicans also prevented a vote on a 
second January 2011 nonunee, Terrence F. Flynn. As a result of these 
filibusters, the NLRB was facing a calamity brought on by the Supreme 
Court’s 2010 decision in a case called New Process Steel v. NLRB, 130 S. 
Ct. 2635 (2010). The Court there interpreted the National Labor Relations 
Act to require three lawfully participating members to be in place in order 
for the NLRB to act. The anticipated expiration of the 2010 Becker recess 
appointment near the end of 2011 threatened to reduce the Board’s 
membership to two. Thus, on December 14, 2011, President Obama 
withdrew the Becker nomination and forwarded to the Senate nominations 
for Sharon Block and Richard F. Griffin, Jr. When the Senate predictably 
did not act on these nominations by the end of the first session of the 112th 
Congress, Obama gave recess appointments to Block and Griffin—and to 
Terrence F. Flynn—on January 4, 2012.
Three Court of Appeals decisions rendered in 2013 invalidated all of 
these appointments. A panel of the Third Circuit voted 2-1 in NLRB v. New 
Vista Nursing and Rehabilitation, 719 F.3d 203 (3d Cir. 2013), that the 
Becker appointment was unconstitutional because, as that court read the 
recess appointments clause, it permitted intersession recess appointments
